MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF VISTRA CORP. 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 2131 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) hereby moves to answer 
and answers the comments filed on April 23, 2025, by the North American Electric Reliability 
Corporate (“NERC”), Americans for a Clean Energy Grid (“ACEG”), Organization of PJM States 
(“OPSI”), and Public Interest Organizations (“PIOs”) in response to the Commission’s February 
 
1  
18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2024).

20, 2025 Order (“Show Cause Order”)2 and PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) answer (“PJM 
Answer”).3  
I. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
Although the Commission’s procedural rules generally do not allow answers to answers, 
the Commission may permit them for good cause.4  The Commission frequently accepts answers 
that clarify the issues before the Commission, ensure a complete record, or otherwise assist the 
Commission in its decision-making.5  Vistra respectfully requests that the Commission accept this 
answer to clarify certain issues and assist the Commission with its decision-making. 
II. 
ANSWER 
The record in this proceeding provides strong support for the Commission to set a 
replacement rate to require PJM to accommodate behind-the-meter co-located load. There is 
general agreement that there is a need for PJM to accommodate new, large loads to support our 
national security and economic growth.6  There is also a general consensus that PJM’s current

Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49 (filed Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”).

18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (“An answer may not be made to a protest, an answer, a motion for oral argument, or 
a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”). 
5  
See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 182 FERC ¶ 61,073, at P 13 (2023) (accepting answers to answers that 
“provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process”); New Fortress Energy LLC, 174 FERC ¶ 
61,207, at P 7 (2021) (accepting answers because they provided information that assisted the Commission’s decision-
making process); Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) (accepting answers that “clarify the 
concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in our decision making”); Saltville Gas Storage Co., L.L.C., 
164 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 n.6 (2018) (accepting answers that “assist the Commission in understanding the issues 
raised, and will ensure a complete record”). 
6  
See, e.g., Comments of Chevron U.S.A. Inc, Docket No. EL25-49, at 2-4 (filed April 23, 2025); Answer of 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. EL25-49, at 3 (filed April 23, 2025) (“Constellation Comments”); 
Comments of Advanced Energy United, Docket No. EL25-49, at 2 (filed April 23, 2025); Comments of the Data 
Center Coalition, Docket No. EL25-49, at 1-2 (filed April 23, 2025); Comments of the Edison Electric Institute, 
Docket No. EL25-49, at 3-4 (filed April 23, 2025); Comments of the Business Council for Sustainable Energy, Docket 
No. EL25-49, at 2 (filed April 23, 2025); Comments of Electricity Consumers Resource Council, Docket No. EL25-
49, at 10.

-4- 
tariff does not sufficiently accommodate the co-location of large loads behind a generator’s meter.7  
The disagreement, as distilled by the filed comments, appears to be over whether that lack of 
accommodation of behind-the-meter co-location is lawful.  Some commenters agree with PJM that 
the tariff remains just and reasonable even though it does not accommodate behind-the-meter co-
located load.8  However, consistent with the Show Cause Order and the Susquehanna ISA 
Rehearing Order,9 many commenters recognize that the existing tariff is not just and reasonable 
and/or that the tariff is being implemented in an unduly discriminatory manner.10   
As discussed further below, there is no valid basis to discriminate against behind-the-meter 
co-located load.  Moreover, none of the commenters that support discriminating against behind-
the-meter load provide any analytic support to justify that position.  Their comments rely on vague 
and unsupported assertions that behind-the-meter co-located load raises reliability and resource 
 
7 
See, e.g., Comments of the Independent Market Monitor for PJM, Docket No. EL25-49, at 2 (filed April 23, 2025) 
(“The Market Monitor agrees that clear rules governing all aspects of the addition of large loads are required.”); 
Constellation Comments at 3 (“The Commission was right that the existing PJM Tariff lacks requisite clarity, and this 
has paralyzed co-location efforts and service to data centers.”); Comments of Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, 
Docket No. EL25-49, at 8 (filed April 23, 2025) (“NOVEC Comments”); Comments of Indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners, Docket No. EL2-49, at 4 (filed April 23, 2025) (“Indicated PJM TOs Comments”). 
8  
See NOVEC Comments at 8; Indicated PJM TOs Comments at 4.  
9 
Show Cause Order at P 3 (directing PJM to explain why its tariff remains just and reasonable without provisions 
addressing behind-the-meter co-location or to explain what changes to the tariff would remedy the absence of such 
provisions); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,025, at P 60 (2025) (“Susquehanna ISA Rehearing Order”) 
(“[W]e clarify that the Rejection Order does not prevent entities from filing non-conforming interconnection 
agreements to address matters related to a generator serving co-located load, or prejudge any such future filing.”). 
10 
See, e.g., Constellation Comments at 3; Comments of BrightNight Power Marketing, LLC, Docket No. EL25-49, 
at 3; Comments of Electric Power Supply Association, Docket No. EL25-49, at 2-3 (filed April 23, 2025); Comments 
of Solar Energy Industries Association, Docket No. EL25-49, at 5 (filed April 23, 2025); Comments of Talen Energy 
Corporation, Docket No. EL25-49, at 12 (filed April 23, 2025); see also Comments of Engie North America, Inc., 
Docket No. EL25-49, at 4-5 (filed April 23, 2025) (explaining that the “current tools in PJM’s existing tariff” are 
inadequate); Comments of PJM Industrial Customer Coalition, Docket No. EL25-49, at 7 (filed April 23, 2025) 
(“Indicated TO’s proposed approach is also unduly discriminatory.”).

-5- 
adequacy concerns.11  To contrast, Vistra’s initial comments included an affidavit by Dr. Roy 
Shanker, which provided a robust and analytically sound assessment of the various configurations 
in which new large loads can be added to the system.12  Dr. Shanker found that Options 4 and 5 
are “dominant” configurations, in that they provide benefits to all parties, including other market 
participants, when compared to other potential load configurations, such as Option 1.13  
In its initial comments, Vistra suggested a specific replacement rate to ensure that the tariff 
accommodates Option 4 and 5 configurations in a just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory manner.14  That proposal would ensure that co-location configurations that fit 
within Options 4 and 5 pay their fair share and that other customers are not harmed.  The 
Commission can and should adopt that replacement rate quickly to remedy undue discrimination 
and ensure that PJM accommodates Options 4 and 5 in a just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory manner.  Vistra also continues to believe that Options 6-8 should be further 
explored to provide customers with flexibility to engage in other types of beneficial transactions.  
However, each of these configurations also appears likely to require more involved tariff 
modifications than those needed for Options 4 and 5.  The Commission should direct PJM to 
engage with stakeholders to implement further reforms to facilitate Options 6-8.   
Beyond the general issues discussed above, this Answer addresses certain specific issues 
raised in the record, including the reliability concerns associated with the addition of new large 
 
11 
See, e.g., NOVEC Comments at 11 (“If co-location arrangements like the configuration advanced by the 
Constellation complaint are permitted, they will present reliability challenges.”); Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc., 
Docket No. EL25-49, at 2-3 (filed April 23, 2025) (arguing that front-of-the-meter co-located loads are “a better 
alternative for reliability and resource adequacy[.]”). 
12 
Comments of Vistra Corp., Docket No. EL25-49, Attach. A, Affidavit of Dr. Roy J. Shanker, PhD on Behalf of 
Vistra Corp. (filed April 23, 2025) (“Dr. Shanker Aff.”). 
13 
Id. PP 52-70. 
14 
See Comments of Vistra Corp., Docket No. EL25-49, at 22-31 (filed April 23, 2025) (“Vistra Initial Comments”).

-6- 
loads, the transparency of the necessary study process, and improvements to PJM’s load 
forecasting practices.  As discussed below, the reliability concerns raised in the docket relate to all 
new large loads, not just those that are co-located with a generator.  Therefore, such concerns do 
not justify discrimination against behind-the-meter co-located loads.  Concerns about the 
transparency of the necessary study process are reasonable, but can be addressed in a 
straightforward manner, by posting necessary study results online in a manner similar to other 
interconnection study results (and with appropriate measures to protect confidential or sensitive 
information).  These concerns do not justify discrimination against behind-the-meter co-located 
loads, nor do they require an overhaul of the necessary study process itself.  Finally, Vistra agrees 
with the suggestions made in the record to improve PJM’s load forecasting process.  In particular, 
ACEG’s proposal to require new large loads to make substantial financial commitments before 
they can be included in PJM’s load forecast would help prevent the inclusion of duplicative load 
interconnection requests in the load forecast.  Development of such a reform would be a natural 
fit within a separate, broader proceeding focused on standardizing the transmission-level load 
interconnection process, which Vistra also suggested in its initial comments.   
A. The Reliability Concerns Raised in Comments Apply to All New Large Loads, 
Regardless of Whether They Are Co-Located  
NERC’s comments provided insight into its recent “initiatives addressing large loads.”15  
To provide further context regarding these reliability concerns, attached to this Answer is an 
affidavit by Steven Herling, PJM’s former VP of Planning, an electrical engineer with 30 years of 
experience with reliability analyses in PJM.16  As Mr. Herling explains, the reliability concerns 
 
15 
Comments of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, Docket No. EL25-49, at 2-10 (filed April 23, 
2025) (“NERC Comments”). 
16 
Affidavit of Steven R. Herling on Behalf of Vistra Corp., Attach. A (“Herling Aff.”).

-7- 
that NERC flagged relate to the voltage sensitivity of new large loads.17  This voltage sensitivity, 
however, “is not a co-location issue,” because it is “equally, or perhaps even more appliable to 
front-of-the-meter interconnections of large data centers, such as contemplated in PJM’s Option 
1.”18  In fact, the particular incident that NERC discussed in Attachment 2 does not appear to have 
involved any co-located data centers.  There is no reason to believe that a behind-the-meter co-
located data center would have worsened this event; in fact, co-location may actually make such 
events less likely because “co-located generators are, themselves, a voltage source with automatic 
voltage regulators, reducing the likelihood that grid disturbances will exceed the threshold 
associated with voltage-sensitive data center loads.”19  Nonetheless, NERC concluded that the 
event “did not cause significant operating issues with the grid.”20 
Minimizing any reliability concerns associated with the co-location of large loads would 
incorporate the same processes and studies utilized to address all other reliability concerns.  As 
Mr. Herling explains, “the modeling elements required to perform power flow, short circuit, and 
dynamic analysis for the various co-location options proposed by PJM are all knowable and any 
operational actions included in PJM’s proposed options are readily modeled.”21  The necessary 
study process includes all of the same models and analytic tools to evaluate contingencies that are 
used in RTEP studies.22  The reliability impacts of new large loads, either alone or in combination 
with a generator, are knowable and can be addressed by proper coordination between PJM, the

Id. PP 15, 21. 
18 
Id. P 21. 
19 
Id.

21 
Herling Aff. at P 19.

-8- 
applicable transmission owner, and the co-located load customer.  This type of coordination is not 
novel in managing reliability impacts of new load of all types.23  NERC recommends that PJM 
should ensure the availability of data and information to support reliability analysis, coordination, 
load balancing, and accurate modeling for co-located large loads.  These recommendations are 
sensible, but there is nothing groundbreaking or new about them.24  Sufficient data and information 
sharing has always been necessary to study the reliability of any new addition on the grid.  Any 
new requirements must apply to all new large loads, not just those that are co-located with a 
generator.   
The existence of reliability concerns related to new, large loads in general does not justify 
prohibiting or delaying the addition of behind-the-meter load.  In fact, as NERC explained: 
Proximity between large loads and power generation sources can 
reduce energy loss while improving transmission reliability.  This 
co-location fosters improved coordination, leading to better load 
management and reduced strain on the BPS . . . NERC noted that 
nuclear power is a particularly advantageous resource for co-located 
large loads due to its inherent high-capacity factor, load-carrying 
ability, and steady performance even in extreme weather 
conditions.25  
 
While transmission owners argue against behind-the-meter co-location, despite its 
reliability benefits compared to Option 1 configurations, transmission owners are moving full 
steam ahead interconnecting new front-of-the-meter large loads.  For example, Exelon utilities 
recently announced on an earnings call that their load interconnection queue includes 16 GW of 
 
23 
See id. P 22. 
24 
Id. 
25 
NERC Comments at 6.

-9- 
new large loads that have already paid deposits.26  Exelon expects to connect 1.6 GW of that load 
by 2028, 5.3 GW by 2030, and 12 GW by 2034.27  Exelon anticipates that these front-of-the-meter 
load interconnections will trigger up to $15 billion in transmission upgrades,28 which will go 
directly into Exelon’s rate base.29  Given that front-of-the-meter large loads raise similar reliability 
concerns as behind-the-meter co-located loads, one can infer that these reliability concerns are not 
insurmountable.  It would be unduly discriminatory to permit front-of-the-meter arrangements and 
prohibit or delay co-location arrangements based on alleged reliability concerns.  
Mr. Herling also provided additional detail about the necessary study process, which 
illustrates that it sufficiently assesses the reliability of behind-the-meter co-located loads, using the 
same models and analytic tools as RTEP studies.30  Some commenters, however, raised questions 
regarding the transparency of the necessary study process for interconnecting new large loads.31  
While these concerns are reasonable, there is a straightforward solution.  PJM posts other 
interconnection study results on a publicly available website.32  PJM could post necessary study 
results there as well, subject to appropriate confidentiality protections for Critical Energy/Electric 
Infrastructure Information and commercially sensitive information, like the identity of the co-

-10- 
located load customer.  These concerns do not require an overhaul of the necessary study process, 
nor do they justify discrimination against the addition of behind-the-meter co-located load.  Rather, 
they can be quickly adopted through surgical tariff revisions similar to those Vistra identified in 
its initial comments. 
B. Generation Asset Owners Should Not Be Prohibited from Maximizing the Use of 
Their Assets 
NOVEC argued that nuclear power plants should not be permitted to serve new large loads 
because they were “largely constructed by or for vertically integrated utilities who funded the 
projects from cost-of-service rates collected by captive retail customers.”33  NOVEC states that it 
“agrees in principle that owners of generation assets should be able to seek to maximize the 
beneficial ownership of those assets,” but asserts that the Commission should reject the co-location 
of large loads at these generating facilities “because the Federal Power Act is a consumer-
protection statute.”34  
Vistra agrees with the principle that owners of generation assets should be able to seek to 
maximize the beneficial ownership of those assets.  PJM may not prohibit sellers from seeking 
beneficial bilateral arrangements in an effort to commandeer the sellers’ resources for the PJM 
capacity market.35  Attempts to do so may even rise to a regulatory taking.36  Moreover, NOVEC’s 
 
33 
NOVEC Comments at 15. 
34 
Id. at 16. 
35 
See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 178 FERC ¶ 61,121, at P 97 (2022) (“If a seller deems PJM’s capacity market 
rules undesirable, it can elect to pursue selling its capacity through other avenues, including via bilateral contracts 
within PJM, external sales outside of PJM, and other arrangements.”). 
36 
See ISO New England, Inc., 135 FERC ¶ 61,029, at P 255 (2011) (rejecting regulatory takings arguments in large 
part because “resources are not compelled to participate in the [ISO-NE capacity market.]”); see also Palazzolo v. 
Rhode Island, 533 U.S. 606, 617–18 (2001) (listing factors relevant to determining whether there is a taking, including 
“the regulation’s economic effect on the [property owner], the extent to which the regulation interferes with reasonable 
investment-backed expectations, and the character of the government action.”); Hodel v. Irving,  481 U.S. 704, 716

-11- 
argument rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of the impacts of co-location on other 
consumers.  As Dr. Roy Shanker previously explained, when compared to an appropriate 
comparison case, Option 4 and 5 configurations provide significant benefits to other market 
participants, both in terms of planning reliability and energy and capacity market prices.37  
Specifically, Dr. Shanker explained that in an Option 4 case, Network Integration Transmission 
Service (“NITS”) costs for other ratepayers remain the same where the parties to the co-location 
arrangement pay for all necessary upgrades; to contrast, in an Option 1 configuration, NITS costs 
for other ratepayers could increase because the costs of transmission facilities would be socialized 
to the entire rate base.38  Dr. Shanker explained that LMPs would be the same in both an Option 4 
and Option 1 case.39  Dr. Shanker also explained that while capacity prices increase in both Option 
4 and Option 1 cases, capacity prices increase more in the Option 1 case than the Option 4 case.40  
NOVEC has provided no analytic basis for its conclusions that co-location is unfair to existing 
ratepayers.  NOVEC’s vague and analytically flawed assertions about consumer protection do not 
justify prohibiting owners of an asset from seeking the most beneficial use of those assets. 
Additionally, as Constellation explained, the premise underlying NOVEC’s argument 
ignores that fact that these “generating resources were sold by most utilities to merchant owners 
over 20 years ago,” at which point merchant owners assumed all risks associated with the 
 
(1987) (federal regulation constituted a taking where it abrogated essential property rights, even though the property 
owners retained other rights, because “the right to pass on property . . . has been part of the Anglo-American legal 
system since feudal times.”); Yancey v. United States, 915 F.2d 1534, 1541 (Fed. Cir. 1990) (noting that regulatory 
taking precedent does not create “an automatic numerical barrier preventing compensation, as a matter of law, in cases 
involving a smaller percentage diminution in value.”).

-12- 
generating facility.41  There are many merchant generators that were once built by a vertically 
integrated utility.  The merchant owners of these plants have always been able to choose how to 
operate their assets, whether that involves capacity market participation or not.  Nuclear plants are 
no different.  Moreover, even under previous the rate-base model, “consumers paid for service, 
not for assets.”42  There is no reason that rates paid to a vertically integrated utility over 20 years 
ago should prevent a private merchant generator from seeking beneficial commercial arrangements 
for facilities that it now owns.  Nor would doing so even benefit ratepayers, as explained above.   
C. Reforms to Load Forecasting Are Warranted, But Should Occur Through a 
Standardized Load Interconnection Process 
ACEG proposed improvements to PJM’s load forecasting process.  Specifically, ACEG 
proposed to require load-serving entities and electric distribution companies that request load 
adjustments demonstrate that any new large loads interconnections are backed by stringent 
financial commitments.  ACEG asserts that the additional financial commitments would not 
impose a new FERC-jurisdictional rate.  Rather, ACEG’s proposal contemplates that these reforms 
occurring primarily through retail tariffs, with “[m]inimal changes to BPM Manual 19.”43   
Vistra agrees that requiring such financial commitments would help improve the accuracy 
of PJM’s load forecasting by disincentivizing load customers from submitting multiple duplicative 
interconnection requests.  However, while Vistra agrees with the overall proposal, Vistra submits 
that these reforms would constitute a FERC-jurisdictional rate—not a retail rate—and, under the 
Commission’s rule of reason, should be placed in the PJM tariff rather than a business practice 
 
41 
Constellation Comments at 107. 
42 
Id. at 108. 
43 
Comments of Americans for a Clean Energy Grid, Docket No. EL25-49, at 8 (filed April 23, 2025).

-13- 
manual.44  As Vistra explained in its initial comments, load interconnection is within the 
Commission’s jurisdiction over the interstate transmission system.45  Load forecasting and the 
requirement to provide additional financial security in the transmission-level load interconnection 
process similarly fall under the Commission’s transmission jurisdiction46 and is a matter “readily 
susceptible of specification” that significantly affects the rates for service.47  Vistra encourages the 
Commission to explore this issue in a separate proceeding focused on standardized transmission-
level load interconnection. 
III. 
Conclusion 
Responses to PJM’s Answer to the Show Cause Order provide a strong record for the 
Commission to act quickly to implement a replacement rate that ensures PJM accommodates 
behind-the-meter co-located load in a just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory manner.  
There is no valid basis to discriminate against behind-the-meter co-located load given that the 
reliability issues of new large loads apply regardless of the specific configuration in which they 
are added to the system.  Based on Dr. Shanker’s analysis of behind-the-meter co-located loads 
against a proper comparison case,48 and Mr. Herling’s conclusions that the relevant reliability 
concerns are equally or even more applicable to non-co-located large loads,49 it is clear that co-
 
44 
See Energy Storage Ass’n v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 162 FERC ¶ 61,296, at P 103 (2018) (“[P]rovisions 
that ‘significantly affect rates, terms, and conditions’ of service, are readily susceptible of specification, and are not 
generally understood in a contractual agreement must be included in a tariff, while items better classified as 
implementation details may be included only in the business practice manual.”).  
45 
See Vistra Initial Comments at 38. 
46  Vistra asserts that the Commission has a second basis for exercising jurisdiction over load forecasting because,

sale of electric energy.

-14- 
location is part of the solution for reliably serving new loads without adversely impacting current 
customers.  Furthermore, concerns about the transparency of the necessary study process can be 
addressed through narrow reforms to ensure that the results of such studies are posted in a manner 
consistent with other interconnection studies.  None of these issues prevent the Commission from 
expeditiously implementing a replacement rate to remedy undue discrimination and ensure PJM 
facilitates Options 4 and 5 configurations.  The record also indicates that the Commission should 
(a) direct PJM to initiate a stakeholder process to determine what tariff revisions would be needed 
to accommodate Options 6-8, and (b) open a proceeding to explore standardized transmission-
level load interconnection procedures, which could include reforms to improve load forecasting 
through financial commitments.

AFFIDAVIT OF STEVEN R. HERLING 
I. 
QUALIFICATIONS AND PURPOSE OF AFFIDAVIT 
 
1. 
My name is Steven R. Herling.  I am currently President of Herling Power Grid Consulting, 
Inc. (“HPGC”), which provides consulting services related to planning, operational, and regulatory 
issues facing the electric power industry.  My business address is 513 William Salesbury Drive, 
Downingtown, PA 19335.  Through HPGC, I have served as a subcontractor to other consulting 
firms, such as The Brattle Group and Charles River Associates.  I have advised clients on generator 
and merchant transmission interconnection issues as well as a range of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
(“PJM”) Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) process issues. 
2. 
In July 2020, I retired from PJM, where I had been employed since May 1990.  At PJM, I held 
a number of positions in the Operations and Planning Divisions and was promoted to Vice President 
of Planning in May 2004.  While at PJM, I contributed to or led initiatives that resulted in a wide 
range of milestone achievements in PJM’s evolution and growth as a regional transmission 
organization (“RTO”), including the creation of the RTEP process, the development of procedures

2 
 
and standard terms and conditions for generation and merchant transmission interconnections, the 
development of the competitive transmission process, and the reliability and resource adequacy 
aspects of successive integrations of additional control areas that more than doubled the size of the 
PJM market area.  In addition to my work for PJM, I contributed to a wide range of activities for the 
North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) and served on various regional industry 
working groups and committees addressing reliability and planning matters. 
3. 
Prior to joining PJM, I worked for the General Public Utilities Service Corporation (“GPU”) 
for three years in systems operations, where I was responsible for dispatcher training and 
certification, operations and planning activities, and energy management system and operational 
support tools.  Prior to GPU, I worked for the American Electric Power Service Corporation (“AEP”) 
for eight years in bulk transmission planning.  In that position, I performed a range of power system 
analyses related to the AEP 765 kV transmission system, generator and circuit breaker dynamic 
modeling, and the mechanical behavior of turbine-generator shaft systems. 
4. 
I hold a Bachelor of Science in Electric Power Engineering and a Master of Engineering in 
Electric Power Engineering, both from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.  Please refer to my resume 
attached as Exhibit B. 
5. 
I have testified on a number of occasions in proceedings before the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“FERC”), as well as various state commissions, and legislative task forces, 
on matters relating to system planning and reliability issues.  I have also testified in transmission line 
Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (“CPCN”) proceedings in Pennsylvania, Maryland, 
West Virginia, Virginia, and New Jersey, and I have testified in a transfer of ownership case for a 
public utility in Kentucky.

3 
 
6. 
I have been asked by Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) to provide an affidavit that discusses the 
concerns raised by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and the North American Electric Reliability 
Organization (“NERC”) with respect to the reliability impacts of the interconnection of large co-
located loads to the grid and how those concerns can reasonably be managed.  This affidavit and the 
opinions expressed herein are based on my experience in the field of electric power system planning, 
operation, and regulation and my knowledge of the electric power industry.  My opinions and 
analyses are subject to change if additional information becomes available. 
II. 
DESCRIPTION OF CO-LOCATION PROJECT OPTIONS 
 
7. 
There are a number of potential options for the interconnection of co-location projects to the 
grid, involving different physical configurations and different means by which the co-located load 
will interact with the grid.  In its March 24, 2025 Answer in the above-captioned docket, PJM 
presents eight such options.  PJM Option 1 is not, in fact, a co-location configuration, but 
contemplates load connected to the grid at a separate point of interconnection from any generator. 
8. 
The remaining PJM options all involve load co-located with generation at the same point of 
interconnection.  Two of the options include relaying that will prevent delivery of energy from the 
grid following the loss of the co-located generating resource.  For example, Option 4 relies on a direct 
connection to co-located generation facility for the delivery of energy without reliance on grid 
transmission facilities.  Some of the PJM options also contemplate the ability of the co-located load to 
take interruptible service or participate as a Demand Response resource, thereby serving as a tool for 
operators to manage operational emergencies.

4 
 
9. 
The design elements of these configurations and the associated operational/market behaviors 
are all well understood and able to be modeled in planning and operations analyses.  
III. 
RELIABILITY ISSUES RAISED BY PJM AND NERC 
10. 
In discussing their proposed options for co-location, PJM describes the various studies that 
may be performed to ensure compliance with applicable reliability criteria.1  As relevant here, PJM 
explained that it performs a Necessary Study when a generator is involved and the co-location project 
involves a modification to the generator’s interconnection.  The Necessary Study is also reviewed by 
the applicable transmission owner.  
11. 
PJM goes on to describe the analyses that comprise the Necessary Study as including 
generation deliverability, N-1 and N-1-1 thermal and voltage studies, special protection systems 
review, baseline stability, and, if applicable, a nuclear plant interface requirements voltage analysis.2   
12. 
PJM also explains the other studies used to integrate new large loads in other configurations 
include 1) a “Transmission Owner retail load integration study,” performed by the local transmission 
owner to identify local upgrades needed to reliably accommodate the load based on the planning 
criteria of that local transmission owner, 2) a “PJM Do No Harm study,” to evaluate whether 
upgrades identified by the local transmission owner will adversely impact the reliability of the 
Transmission System, and 3) Regional Transmission Expansion Planning (RTEP) studies when an 
aggregation of large load additions could possibly trigger regional transmission needs.3 
13. 
In their response to FERC question D. iii., PJM states “In response to this question’s specific 
prompt about dynamic response models, today, PJM conducts dynamic studies for co-located load 
projects. All applicable North American Reliability Corporation (“NERC”), PJM, and Transmission 
 
1 PJM Answer at 7. 
2 Id. at 49. 
3 Id. at 6-8.

5 
 
Owner-specific contingencies and criteria are evaluated. For such dynamic studies, co-located loads 
are modeled in detail within both power flow and dynamic models.”4  
14. 
PJM raises one concern with respect to co-location projects interconnected through its Option 
4 or Option 5.  PJM Options 4 and 5 include relaying that will prevent delivery of energy from the 
grid following the loss of the co-located generating resource.  PJM raises the concern that “it is 
possible to develop a special protection scheme that could disconnect the load if the local generator 
trips. This scheme could be developed with sufficient redundancy to help better ensure activation. 
However, it is always possible that the protection system could misoperate, be disabled, or degrade.”5  
15. 
NERC raises reliability concerns related to the voltage sensitivity of co-location loads and the 
potential for disconnection from the grid and transfer to backup generation.6  As an example, NERC 
cites the loss of approximately 1,500 MW of load following a 230 kV transmission line fault when 
the line locked out after three auto-reclose attempts.7  The loss occurred when voltage-sensitive data 
center load at 60 different load points across 25 different substations was automatically disconnected 
from the grid.8  NERC refers to a Commission comment in its Show Cause Order, suggesting that 
system operators may lack sufficient information and transient stability models to perform reliability 
analysis on co-located large loads.9  
16. 
Based on these concerns, NERC recommends “that the Commission and industry continue 
examining specific reliability implications of co-located large loads. NERC also recommends that the 
Commission and industry consider requirements for data or information sharing, to support system 
 
4 Id. at 53. 
5 Id. at 44. 
6 NERC Comments at 3-10. 
7 Id. at 8. 
8 Id., Attach. A, at 4. 
9 NERC Comments at 7.

6 
 
operators in performing reliability analyses as well as coordination, load balancing, and accurate 
modeling for co-located large loads.”10  
IV. 
OBSERVATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS 
17. 
PJM and the PJM transmission owners currently perform a wide range of analyses to establish 
compliance of the grid with all NERC, PJM, and transmission owner planning criteria.  These studies 
span the entire range of power flow, short circuit, and dynamics analyses and have been performed, 
collaboratively, for decades, since the inception of PJM as an Independent System Operator.   
18. 
Through the Necessary Study process described above, PJM has the ability to evaluate all 
aspects of a co-location project to ensure that it is designed such that the grid remains reliable, 
consistent with all applicable criteria.  The Necessary Study relies on the same transmission system, 
generation, and load models that PJM uses throughout all aspects of the RTEP process.  It utilizes all 
of the same analytical tools and evaluates all of the same contingency sets to test compliance against 
all of the same reliability criteria. 
19. 
The modeling elements required to perform power flow, short circuit, and dynamics analyses 
for the various co-location options, proposed by PJM, are all knowable and any operational actions 
included in PJM’s proposed options are readily modeled.  PJM and the PJM transmission owners 
have the ability to collaborate to perform all of the analyses required to ensure the continued 
reliability of the PJM grid.   
20. 
With respect to PJM’s concerns about potential failure of a special protective system, it is 
worth noting that PJM plans, in its RTEP analyses, for N-1 conditions followed by a single protection 
system failure, such as a stuck breaker.  In this instance, a stuck breaker becomes a second 
contingency.  Based on my experience with the RTEP, the solution to stuck breaker criteria violations 
 
10 Id. at 3.

7 
 
is to add a redundant series breaker, making the failure of both breakers following an N-1 event a 
third contingency.  PJM does not plan for or require upgrades for such third contingencies, nor would 
it be reasonable to do so.  Assuming that the protection system associated with an Option 4 or 5 co-
location project is fully redundant, it is unreasonable to treat the failure of both primary and 
secondary relay system facilities following the loss of a generator as anything other than a third 
contingency. 
21. 
It is also important to note that the voltage-sensitivity issue underlying the 1,500 MW load 
loss event cited by NERC is not a co-location issue.  Nothing in the NERC Comments or the attached 
materials suggests that any of the data centers involved in the event were co-located with generating 
resources.  The voltage sensitivity issue at the core of the discussion is equally, or perhaps even more 
applicable to front-of-meter interconnections of large data centers, such as contemplated in PJM’s 
Option 1.  Co-located generators are, themselves, a voltage source with automatic voltage regulators, 
reducing the likelihood that grid disturbances will exceed the threshold associated with voltage-
sensitive data center loads.  The loss occurred because the loads transferred from the grid to their own 
uninterruptible power supply (“UPS”) systems in order to protect data center cooling equipment, not 
because of any interaction with co-located generation.11  
22. 
NERC’s recommendation to continue studying these issues and engage in information sharing 
is sensible.  Coordination of study efforts between PJM and the PJM transmission owners has always 
been a foundational element of the PJM planning process and must continue for the grid to remain 
reliable and for customer needs to be met in a timely, fair and non-discriminatory manner.  Consistent 
with NERC’s stated concerns, PJM should have access to the data and information required to 
support operational actions and the performance of reliability analyses.  PJM as the planner and 
 
11 NERC Comments, Attach. B, at 4.

8 
 
operator of the grid requires detailed data for large voltage-sensitive loads, whether they are co-
located with generation sources or interconnected to the grid separate from any generator. 
23. 
This concludes my affidavit.

9 
 
VERIFICATION 
 
 
I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing Affidavit is true and correct to the best 
of my knowledge, information, and belief.
